mechanism_reasoning: up EED is an obligate, non-catalytic subunit of PRC2: its WD40 domain binds H3K27me3 and allosterically stimulates the EZH2 methyltransferase, which sustains the repressive mark. Losing EED therefore collapses PRC2 activity and erases H3K27me3 across Polycomb-repressed loci — the order matters: EED loss first, H3K27me3 depletion second, and only then transcriptional de-repression. Scin is a CDX2 target that carries Polycomb repression in this context, so once the H3K27me3 lock is removed the locus becomes accessible and permissive, letting the existing/available CDX2 pool bind and activate it rather than any new CDX2 activity being required. Net effect: derepression plus CDX2-driven activation both push Scin in the same direction, so expression goes up relative to the matched unperturbed control.

up Loss of EED abolishes PRC2 catalytic activity, so H3K27me3 is no longer deposited at the Slc26a6 locus and the repressive, compacted chromatin state cannot be maintained. With that block removed, the pre-bound activator CDX2 can engage its coactivators (e.g., p300/CBP, MED1) and drive transcriptional initiation; H3K27me3 loss comes first, followed by increased chromatin accessibility and then elevated Slc26a6 mRNA. Ectopic activation can also follow from redistribution of H3K27me3 and compensatory H3K4me3/H3K27ac gain at the promoter, reinforcing the upregulation.

down TP63 is a p53-family transcription factor that acts canonically as a sequence-specific activator, binding response elements in the regulatory regions (promoter/enhancer) of its target genes and recruiting co-activators (p300/CBP, mediator) to drive RNA polymerase II initiation. Because ANKRD27 is listed as a TP63-regulated target, the inferred regulatory link is positive: TP63 occupancy supplies activating input to the ANKRD27 locus. When TP63 is lost or reduced, that activating input is removed — the response elements are no longer occupied, co-activator recruitment falls, and the basal transcriptional machinery at the ANKRD27 promoter runs at a lower rate. The causal order is therefore: TP63 protein loss (perturbation) → loss of TF occupancy at ANKRD27 regulatory elements → reduced co-activator/Pol II engagement → decreased ANKRD27 mRNA. So relative to the matched unperturbed control, ANKRD27 expression is expected to go down. (Caveat: if the specific mechanism were direct repression rather than activation, the sign would invert; the activator interpretation is the default for this TF–target relationship.)

down TP63 acts as a transcriptional regulator of HNRNPA1 in this context, so it functions upstream in the causal chain: TP63 binds and drives HNRNPA1 expression, and HNRNPA1 is the downstream effector. When TP63 is lost or reduced, that activating input is removed — fewer TP63 molecules occupy the HNRNPA1 promoter/enhancer, transcription initiation drops, and mature HNRNPA1 mRNA and protein levels fall over the following hours. The matched unperturbed control, which retains TP63, therefore sits at the higher basal level, and the net direction of change is a decrease. This ordering matters: TP63 loss is the primary event, reduced transcriptional output is the immediate consequence, and the drop in HNRNPA1 abundance is the readout — not the reverse. The main caveat is that if the mechanism were instead TP63-mediated repression (or if a compensatory paralog sustained transcription), the sign would flip; the default activator assumption is what makes the direction "down."

down TP63 is a p53-family sequence-specific transcription factor that acts as a transcriptional activator at its target promoters and enhancers. In this context the regulatory edge is annotated as TP63 → HNRNPL, meaning TP63 provides positive input to HNRNPL expression. The causal chain runs: TP63 loss-of-function (CRISPR knockout/knockdown) → loss of TP63 protein occupancy at its response elements in the HNRNPL promoter/enhancer → reduced recruitment of coactivators and RNA polymerase II and less productive transcription initiation → decreased HNRNPL mRNA, and consequently decreased hnRNPL protein. Because the perturbation removes an activating regulator rather than a repressor, the target moves in the same direction as the regulator — down. The effect is expected in the matched control context, so the comparison is against unperturbed cells of the same cell type and condition, where TP63 is intact and continues to drive basal HNRNPL transcription. Only if TP63 were acting as a repressor at this locus (or if a compensatory paralog such as TP53/TP73 or another hnRNP compensated) would the direction reverse; under the standard annotation of an activating regulatory edge, the expected direction is down.

down TP63 is the transcriptional regulator here, and in the absence of any repression mechanism the default regulatory relationship is activation: p63 binds the promoter/enhancer of its target and drives its transcription. L3HYPDH (trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline dehydratase, a proline-catabolism enzyme) therefore sits downstream as a positively controlled target. The causal order is: TP63 protein is lost or reduced → occupancy of the L3HYPDH regulatory element drops → the activating signal at that promoter falls → L3HYPDH mRNA (and subsequently protein) declines relative to the matched unperturbed control. Rise would only be expected if TP63 were acting as a repressor (i.e., if loss relieved direct repression, or if loss triggered a compensatory pathway that secondarily induced L3HYPDH), and no such mechanism is specified for this pair; the straightforward activator-loss logic gives down.

down TP63 is a positive regulator of NABP2: p63 family proteins (TAp63/ΔNp63α) occupy p63 response elements in target promoters/enhancers and recruit co-activators such as p300/CBP plus the basal transcriptional machinery, so NABP2 transcription depends on continued p63 occupancy. Order of events after the perturbation: TP63 loss → the activator is no longer bound at the NABP2 regulatory region and co-activator recruitment/active chromatin marks are lost → reduced RNA Pol II initiation and elongation at the NABP2 locus → falling NABP2 mRNA and, consequently, lower hSSB1 protein (which is also short-lived and further destabilized when the DNA-damage-response context that normally supports it is lost). The key mediator is therefore the p63-dependent transactivation input itself, not an indirect signaling relay, so the matched control comparison shows NABP2 going down rather than up.

down TP63 acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional activator at the RPS16 promoter/enhancer, so reducing TP63 removes that activating input. Order of events: TP63 protein levels fall → occupancy of TP63 binding elements upstream of RPS16 decreases → the RPS16 promoter loses its activating stimulus and its transcriptional output drops → mature RPS16 mRNA (and RPS16 protein) declines relative to the matched unperturbed control. The key mediator is TP63 itself acting as the direct trans-activator of RPS16; in its absence, baseline RNA polymerase II initiation and elongation at RPS16 are not maintained at control levels, giving a net decrease rather than a compensatory increase.

down TP63 encodes p63, a p53-family transcription factor that acts canonically as a sequence-specific activator: it binds response elements in the promoters/enhancers of its target genes and recruits coactivators (e.g., p300/CBP) to drive RNA polymerase II initiation. Here TIMM50 — the mitochondrial inner-membrane translocase subunit — is a direct transcriptional target in the TP63 regulatory network, so the causal order is TP63 binding → increased TIMM50 transcription → higher TIMM50 mRNA/protein. Reducing or losing TP63 removes that activating input, so the promoter is no longer occupied and transcription of TIMM50 falls; the readout relative to the matched unperturbed control therefore moves downward. The key mediator of the change is loss of p63 occupancy (and consequent loss of coactivator recruitment) at the TIMM50 locus rather than any post-transcriptional step, meaning the drop should appear at the nascent-transcript/mRNA level first.

down TET2 is a 5-methylcytosine dioxygenase that keeps CpG-rich promoters and enhancers hypomethylated by oxidizing 5mC toward 5hmC and eventual demethylation. Losing TET2 function therefore shifts the epigenome toward hypermethylation, and the ESR1 locus is one of the well-documented targets: with TET2 activity reduced, the ESR1 promoter/enhancer region accumulates 5mC and ESR1 expression falls. Because ESR1 is the upstream activator acting on the ELOVL2 regulatory element in this context, the causal order runs TET2 loss → ESR1 promoter/enhancer hypermethylation → reduced ESR1 protein and occupancy at the ELOVL2 locus → weakened transcriptional activation → lower ELOVL2 mRNA. The mediator is the loss of ESR1-driven transactivation, not a direct effect of TET2 on ELOVL2, so the expected direction relative to the matched unperturbed control is down.

down TET2 is the 5-methylcytosine dioxygenase that keeps CpG dinucleotides at active enhancers and at the regulatory elements of ESR1 in an unmethylated, 5hmC-marked state; its loss (as in Tet2 knockout/haploinsufficiency) causes the ESR1 promoter and enhancer regions to become hypermethylated, so ESR1/ERα is transcriptionally silenced — a reduction seen already at the heterozygous dose and accompanied by global 5mC gain. TET2 loss additionally strips ERα of its coactivator function, since TET2 occupies the same active enhancers as ERα and its depletion impairs E2-dependent ERα recruitment to those elements, so both the amount of ESR1 and the DNA-binding activity of the remaining ERα fall. Because PTGES is an ESR1/ERα target whose transcription depends on ERα occupancy at its regulatory elements, cutting the upstream ERα input lowers PTGES transcription. The order is therefore: TET2 loss → loss of 5hmC and hypermethylation of ESR1 regulatory DNA → decreased ESR1 expression plus weakened ERα enhancer binding → reduced ERα-driven transactivation of PTGES → PTGES expression down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down TET2 is a 5-methylcytosine dioxygenase whose loss removes the 5hmC intermediate needed for both passive and TDG/BER-dependent active demethylation, so the DNA methylation it normally keeps off regulatory elements accumulates. Two convergent branches push WIPF1 transcription downward. First, TET2 loss drives progressive hypermethylation of active enhancers and estrogen response elements; the resulting 5mC recruits MBD/MeCP2-HDAC complexes, compacts chromatin, and — because TET2 also recruits OGT to maintain HCF1-SET1/COMPASS-dependent H3K4me3 — strips the activating mark that keeps these elements competent, so ERα occupancy at its response elements is impaired and the ERα-driven transcriptional output falls. Second, TET2 in complex with FOXP1 maintains demethylation of ESR1 itself, so its loss additionally lowers ESR1 expression and hence the abundance of the very activator that drives WIPF1. Since ESR1 acts as an activator of the WIPF1-coexpressed module, the order is: TET2 loss → 5hmC loss and enhancer/promoter hypermethylation (plus reduced H3K4me3) → weakened ESR1 expression and ERα binding at its target elements → reduced transcription of ESR1-dependent targets including WIPF1. Down is therefore the expected direction, though the effect should be modest and locus-dependent, since TET2 loss fine-tunes rather than abolishes ERα target transcription.

down ESR1 (estrogen receptor α) acts as a ligand-activated transcription factor that binds estrogen response elements at the CISH regulatory site and recruits coactivators to drive CISH transcription. Removing or reducing that regulatory site abolishes ESR1 occupancy, so the activating input to the CISH promoter/enhancer is lost and the gene is transcribed at a lower rate. The order is: site loss → loss of ESR1 binding and coactivator recruitment → reduced transcriptional initiation → lower steady-state CISH mRNA. In the matched unperturbed control the site is intact, so ESR1 maintains the higher baseline expression; hence CISH goes down relative to that control.

down ESR1 (estrogen receptor α) is a ligand-activated transcription factor that, upon estrogen binding, occupies estrogen response elements within target enhancers and promoters and recruits coactivators (SRC/p300 family) to drive transcription. G0S2 sits downstream of an ESR1-bound regulatory site, so the site is the docking platform through which ERα delivers its activating signal. When that regulatory site is lost or reduced, ERα can no longer be recruited to the locus, coactivator loading and chromatin activation at the G0S2 promoter/enhancer collapse, and the basal and estrogen-induced transcription of G0S2 falls. Order of events: ESR1 binding to the regulatory site → coactivator recruitment and enhancer activation → G0S2 transcription; remove the site and the first step fails, so the terminal step (G0S2 expression) drops relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same context.

Down. Causal chain: ESR1 (ERα) is the activating input at the MMP17 enhancer cluster — the MMP17-1 ERBS carries a full ERE and sits at the top of a hierarchical pair of ER-bound sites, recruiting ERα and establishing the active H3K27ac/accessible chromatin state, with MMP17-2 then binding ERα and contributing to promoter activity. ERα occupancy at those sites is what transmits the estrogen signal to the MMP17 promoter, and MMP17 is strongly induced downstream of that axis (e.g. ~14-fold E2 induction in Ishikawa cells, versus no induction in T-47D where those ERBS lack ER binding and H3K27ac). So removing or reducing ESR1 — or deleting the target regulatory site itself — strips the enhancer of its activator: ER occupancy at the ERE is lost first, enhancer activity and chromatin accessibility collapse, the promoter's activation signal disappears, and MMP17 transcription falls. Order: ESR1 loss → loss of ER at the MMP17 ERBS cluster → loss of enhancer/promoter activation → decreased MMP17 mRNA. (Cell-type context matters: this direction holds in ER-dependent, ERBS-active contexts.)

down GATA1 binds GATA motifs in the regulatory region of Lrrc39 and drives its transcription as part of the erythroid/megakaryocytic gene program. The D218G substitution sits in the N-terminal zinc finger — the domain that stabilizes high-affinity DNA binding and recruits the coregulator machinery (FOG1, the TAL1/SCL–LMO2–LDB1 complex, and CBP/p300 with GATA1's C-terminal finger providing the main transactivation surface). Because D218G is a hypomorphic/loss-of-function change, mutant GATA1 occupies the Lrrc39 promoter/enhancer less efficiently and delivers a weaker transactivation signal, so the order runs: impaired N-finger DNA binding → reduced GATA1 occupancy and coactivator recruitment → less Pol II loading/elongation at Lrrc39 → lower Lrrc39 mRNA. Relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same cellular context, Lrrc39 therefore goes down.

down Rragd is a positively regulated (activated) GATA1 target whose +4 kb regulatory element carries a single GATA motif that GATA1 can only occupy with FOG1/ZFPM1 acting as a chromatin-occupancy facilitator. The D218G substitution sits in the GATA1 N-terminal zinc finger and does not impair DNA binding, but it weakens the GATA1–FOG1 protein–protein interaction; the order of events is therefore: weakened GATA1–FOG1 binding → loss/instability of GATA1 occupancy at the FOG1-dependent Rragd +4 kb element and failure to assemble the activating complex there (FOG1, plus associated coactivators and the GATA1/TAL1–LMO2–LDB1 machinery at erythroid loci) → reduced RNA Pol II loading and lower Rragd transcription. In G1E/G1ME complementation assays, N-finger mutants that disrupt FOG1 binding reduce GATA1-dependent gene activation, and D218G does so in the same direction as wild-type GATA1 but more weakly — this is the mildest FOG1-binding allele, so the reduction in Rragd is expected to be modest in magnitude while still downward. Note the direction holds because the element is an activating, FOG1-dependent site; FOG1-independent GATA1 repression targets would move the opposite way, and here activation is impaired more than repression for D218G.

down GATA1 is the master erythroid transcription factor that directly occupies and activates the erythroid promoter/enhancer of Slc4a1 (Band 3/AE1), so Slc4a1 transcription is a readout of functional GATA1 dosage. The D218G substitution sits in the N-terminal zinc finger and impairs GATA1's DNA-binding/cofactor (FOG1) engagement, producing a hypomorphic, loss-of-function allele (the X-linked dyserythropoietic anemia with thrombocytopenia phenotype). With a crippled activator bound at the Slc4a1 regulatory region, the causal order is: variant → reduced GATA1 transactivation capacity (key mediator: GATA1 itself, acting as the sequence-specific activator at the Slc4a1 locus) → less RNA polymerase II recruitment → lower Slc4a1 mRNA. Hence, relative to matched unperturbed control in the same context, Slc4a1 expression is expected to go down.

down GATA1 R216Q is a hypomorphic missense change in the N‑terminal zinc finger that weakens GATA1's ability to engage palindromic GATA elements and to recruit cofactors such as FOG1. Because the transcription factor acts upstream as an activator of Lrrc39 — the variant protein binds the gene's regulatory region less effectively and/or assembles a less productive activation complex — the rate of Lrrc39 transcription falls, and its steady-state mRNA is therefore lower than in the matched unperturbed control. The order is: variant GATA1 → impaired DNA binding/cofactor recruitment → reduced transactivation at the Lrrc39 locus → decreased Lrrc39 expression.

down Rragd is a GATA1-activated erythroid target (it sits in the list of direct GATA1-activated genes that are especially sensitive to the R216Q substitution), so its expression tracks GATA1's transactivation capacity. GATA1 R216Q is a hypomorphic N-terminal zinc-finger variant: GATA1 still occupies its target sites and still binds FOG1, but the arginine-to-glutamine change at the DNA-binding face abolishes high-affinity binding of the LMO2/LDB1 adaptor and selectively impairs recruitment of the TAL1/SCL activator complex, which is the module used for GATA1-dependent gene activation rather than repression. Because activation (not silencing) is what is lost — roughly a 60% reduction in activation output in erythroid complementation assays — the causal order is: R216Q variant → weakened TAL1/LMO2/LDB1 coactivator recruitment at Rragd regulatory elements → reduced GATA1-driven transactivation → lower Rragd mRNA relative to matched wild-type GATA1.

down GATA1 is a direct transcriptional activator of Slc4a1 (erythroid band 3/AE1): it occupies the GATA motifs in the Slc4a1 promoter and erythroid enhancer and recruits coactivators such as CBP/p300 and the Mediator complex to drive transcription. The R216Q substitution sits in the N-terminal zinc finger, the domain that stabilizes GATA1 on palindromic GATA sites (and mediates FOG1/ZFPM1 interaction), so the mutant protein binds its cognate sites in the Slc4a1 regulatory region less stably. Order of events: R216Q variant → weakened GATA1 DNA occupancy at Slc4a1 cis-elements → loss of coactivator recruitment and reduced promoter/enhancer activity → lower Slc4a1 mRNA. Hence, relative to the matched unperturbed control, Slc4a1 expression decreases.

up SAMD9L is a canonical ΔNp63α/TP63-repressed, anti-proliferative target: TP63 (ΔNp63α) binds the SAMD9L locus and recruits the SRCAP chromatin-remodeling complex, which exchanges H2A/H2A.Z and deposits the histone variant H2A.Z at these sites. The deposited H2A.Z establishes a repressive chromatin state that blocks productive RNA polymerase II elongation, so SAMD9L stays transcriptionally silent. Because H2A.Z deposition is the actual effector of the repression — knockdown of SRCAP subunits or of H2A.Z itself specifically de-represses these TP63-bound genes — reducing H2A.Z removes the repressive mark downstream of TP63, relieving the block on RNAPII and de-repressing SAMD9L. Order of events: TP63 binding → SRCAP-mediated H2A.Z deposition → RNAPII repression; H2A.Z loss breaks the last step, so SAMD9L expression rises relative to the matched control.

down H2A.Z (H2AFZ)-containing nucleosomes flank the nucleosome-depleted regions of active promoters and enhancers and are required for their accessibility and function. Because ZHX2 is a TP63 target, its regulation is expected to run through a TP63-bound promoter/enhancer element, and H2A.Z turnover at that element is what keeps it accessible and competent for transcription-factor engagement. When H2A.Z is lost or reduced, the ordered chain is: reduced H2A.Z deposition/turnover → impaired nucleosome eviction and chromatin accessibility at the ZHX2 regulatory element → weakened TP63 occupancy and loss of TP63-dependent activation → decreased RNA Pol II recruitment/initiation at the ZHX2 promoter → lower ZHX2 mRNA. In other words, H2A.Z acts upstream as a permissive chromatin cofactor for the TP63→ZHX2 regulatory axis, so removing it is expected to decrease, not increase, ZHX2 expression relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down miR-210 is a hypoxia-induced microRNA whose canonical, well-validated target is the iron–sulfur cluster assembly scaffold ISCU. Gaining miR-210 activity loads the RISC/Argonaute2 complex with a guide strand bearing a seed match in the ISCU 3′UTR; pairing there first causes translational repression and then accelerated deadenylation and decay of the ISCU transcript, so within the same hypoxic context the perturbed cells end up with less ISCU mRNA and protein than the matched unperturbed control. The causal order is therefore: miR-210 up → RISC loading → ISCU 3′UTR binding → reduced ISCU translation plus transcript destabilization → lower ISCU output (and consequently poorer Fe–S cluster assembly, the metabolic phenotype miR-210 is known to drive). Note this runs counter to the HIF1A→ISCU arm in your context: HIF1A raises miR-210 transcription, and the microRNA then sets a ceiling on ISCU, so the net direction under a miR-210 gain is downward.

up TWIST1 drives expression of the miR-10b hairpin from the Hox cluster, and mature miR-10b loads into an Argonaute-containing RISC that base-pairs with the HOXD10 3′UTR, recruiting deadenylation and translational repression of that transcript. So the ordering in the intact circuit is TWIST1 → miR-10b → reduced HOXD10 protein and mRNA. Removing or knocking down miR-10b severs the middle link: the HOXD10 transcript is no longer targeted for RISC-mediated silencing, so it accumulates and HOXD10 expression rises relative to the matched control — a classic loss-of-microRNA de-repression, with the effect being post-transcriptional and therefore visible even when the HOXD10 locus itself is not transcriptionally re-activated.

down CA12 (carbonic anhydrase XII) is a canonical estrogen-receptor–driven gene: in ESR1-positive contexts, ligand-bound ESR1 binds estrogen-response elements in the CA12 promoter and directly transactivates it, so the transcription factor acts as a positive regulator upstream of the gene. Removing or reducing ESR1 therefore cuts off that activation input — the promoter loses its activating TF occupancy, coactivator recruitment (e.g., the p160/SRC and p300/CBP complexes) falls, and the CA12 locus shifts toward a less permissive chromatin state. The causal order is: ESR1 loss → loss of ER-driven transactivation at the CA12 promoter → reduced CA12 mRNA and protein. Hence, relative to the matched unperturbed control, CA12 expression is expected to go down.

down FOXC1e is the upstream input for this pair — the regulatory element/regulator through which ESR1 acts on the FOXC1 locus — so it sits above FOXC1 in the causal chain. Removing or reducing it severs that input: less activator is present at the FOXC1 promoter/enhancer, co-activator recruitment and transcription-initiation complex assembly drop, and the rate of FOXC1 transcription falls, so mature FOXC1 mRNA accumulates to a lower steady-state level than in the matched unperturbed control. Order of events: loss of FOXC1e activity → reduced ESR1-dependent activation of the FOXC1 locus → decreased FOXC1 transcription → lower FOXC1 expression. No feedback loop that would restore or overshoot FOXC1 is specified, so the direction is downward.

down GREB1e is an estrogen-receptor–bound enhancer of GREB1, so it acts upstream and positively. ESR1 (ERα) occupies estrogen response elements within GREB1e and, on ligand activation, recruits coactivators (MED1, p300/CBP, SRC family) that sustain enhancer–promoter looping and RNA Pol II loading at the GREB1 promoter. Losing or reducing GREB1e removes that ESR1 docking site, so coactivator recruitment and the enhancer–promoter contact collapse, and GREB1 transcription falls — the regulatory element is the cause, ESR1 binding the key mediator, and reduced GREB1 mRNA the effect, in that order. Hence GREB1 expression is expected to go down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down Perturbation acts directly on the perturbed entity (KCNK5 expression), so the primary, most proximal effect is on KCNK5's own transcript: a loss-or-reduction intervention (CRISPRi/RNAi-style knockdown of the gene or its promoter) lowers KCNK5 mRNA relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same context. No intermediate mediator is required for this step — the causal order is simply perturbation → reduced KCNK5 transcription/transcript level. ESR1 sits upstream as the regulator of KCNK5, but it is not itself the perturbed node here, so its activation status is unchanged and cannot offset the direct loss: if ESR1-dependent activation of the KCNK5 promoter is what maintains baseline expression, removing that output (by knocking down KCNK5) yields a net decrease, not a compensatory increase. The one assumption worth flagging is that the intervention targets KCNK5 itself rather than ESR1 activity; under that reading the expected direction is up, since an activating regulator's loss would de-repress/down-regulate its target. Given the stated perturbed entity, the answer is down.

down NRIP1 is a direct ESR1 (ERα) target: liganded ERα binds estrogen-response elements in the NRIP1 promoter and drives its transcription. Because the perturbation is loss/reduction of NRIP1 itself, the transcript that is being measured is the one being removed — targeted knockdown or CRISPRi of NRIP1 lowers its own mRNA — and any secondary loop reinforces the same direction, since NRIP1 (RIP140) serves as an ERα cofactor whose depletion dampens ERα-dependent transcription of the same promoter. Order: NRIP1 loss → reduced NRIP1 transcript (and reduced ERα-driven NRIP1 promoter activity) → lower NRIP1 expression than the matched unperturbed control.

down ESR1 acts as an activating transcription factor at the P2RY2 locus, binding a cis-regulatory enhancer element (P2RY2e) and recruiting coactivators (e.g., steroid receptor coactivators, p300/CBP) that maintain an open, H3K27ac-marked chromatin state and load RNA polymerase II at the P2RY2 promoter. When that element is lost or reduced, the ESR1-dependent activating input is removed, so the enhancer–promoter looping that sustains constitutive P2RY2 transcription weakens. The causal order is: enhancer loss/reduction → loss of ESR1 binding and coactivator recruitment → reduced chromatin accessibility and Pol II pause release at the promoter → decreased P2RY2 mRNA output relative to the matched unperturbed control. Note the direction assumes the mechanism is activating (the usual case for an estrogen-receptor-bound enhancer driving its target); if ESR1 were instead repressive at this element, the loss-of-element result would flip, so the enhancer's direction of effect — not merely its occupancy — is the key determinant.

down ESR1 (estrogen receptor α) is the direct transcriptional activator of PGR: ligand-bound ERα binds estrogen-response-element half-sites in the PGR promoter/enhancer and recruits coactivators to drive PGR transcription. Reducing ESR1 therefore removes that activating input at the promoter, so PGR mRNA and protein fall — the direction is set by ESR1 acting upstream of PGR, with the loss of ESR1 occurring first and the drop in PGR transcription following as the downstream consequence. This is the classic ERα→PR axis used in breast cancer pathology (loss of ERα signaling, e.g. under endocrine therapy or ESR1 silencing, tracks with reduced PR expression).

down SIAH2 is the perturbed entity itself, so the loss-of-function perturbation (CRISPRi/knockdown/knockout) acts directly on the SIAH2 locus: transcription of SIAH2 mRNA is reduced and, because SIAH2 is an E3 ubiquitin–ligase whose own abundance is short-lived, protein follows quickly. The upstream regulator in this context, ESR1, sits earlier in the chain and drives SIAH2 transcription; any indirect compensation would have to run in the reverse order — loss of SIAH2 relieves its destabilization of ESR1, raising ESR1 and secondarily SIAH2 transcription — but that is a delayed, downstream feedback loop and cannot outrun the primary loss of SIAH2 transcript/protein within the assay window. Net effect relative to the matched unperturbed control: SIAH2 expression decreases.

down ESR1 (ERα) acts as a positive transcriptional regulator of SMAD7 — in ERα-positive settings, ESR1 expression tracks with SMAD7 mRNA and protein (e.g., ESR1 overexpression raises SMAD7 in HCC cells, where ERα cooperates with cofactors at Smad-responsive/ER-responsive regulatory elements). Loss or reduction of ESR1 therefore removes an activating input at the SMAD7 locus: ERα/coactivator occupancy on the SMAD7 promoter-enhancer falls first, SMAD7 transcription decreases next, and SMAD7 mRNA followed by protein drops — the mediator being the ERα–cofactor transcriptional complex itself, not a downstream signaling relay. (The same downward direction holds if the perturbed entity is SMAD7 itself, since a loss-of-function knockdown simply removes SMAD7 transcript.) Physiologically this also unbuttons the negative-feedback arm of TGF-β signaling: with less inhibitory SMAD7 to bind activated TβRI and recruit SMURF1/2 for receptor degradation, SMAD2/3 phosphorylation is de-repressed even as SMAD7 abundance goes down.

down ESR1 encodes ERα, a ligand-dependent nuclear receptor that binds estrogen-response elements in the TFF1 promoter/enhancer and, together with coactivators (e.g. NCOA/SRC family, p300/CBP), recruits RNA polymerase II to drive TFF1 transcription. TFF1 is therefore a canonical positively regulated ERα target, so loss or reduction of the upstream regulator removes that activation and TFF1 transcript levels fall relative to the matched control — the order being ESR1 loss → loss of ERE occupancy and coactivator recruitment → reduced Pol II initiation at the TFF1 promoter → lower TFF1 mRNA. The same downward direction holds if the perturbation instead removes TFF1 transcript directly, since either way the activated ESR1→TFF1 arm is broken before TFF1 output is measured.

up PPARα (PPARA) is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that, upon activation, heterodimerizes with RXR and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in the promoters/enhancers of its target genes. *Angptl4* (fasting-induced adipose factor) carries a functional PPRE and is one of the best-characterized direct PPARα target genes — well documented in liver (and also via PPARβ/δ in other tissues). The causal order is therefore: PPARA activation → PPARα/RXR binding to the *Angptl4* PPRE → increased *Angptl4* transcription → higher Angptl4 mRNA (and secreted ANGPTL4 protein), which then acts as an LPL inhibitor. Because the effect is direct transcriptional activation rather than an indirect feedback arm, acute gain-of-function of PPARA raises *Angptl4* expression relative to the matched unperturbed control.

Up. PPARα (NR1C1) is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor, and Hmgcs2 — the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis — is a canonical PPARα target. Under gain-or-activation conditions the order is: ligand (fasting-derived free fatty acids, or a synthetic agonist such as WY-14643/fenofibrate) binds the PPARα ligand-binding domain → PPARα heterodimerizes with RXR and binds the PPRE (DR1 element) in the Hmgcs2 promoter/enhancer → coactivators (PGC-1α, SRC-1) are recruited and chromatin is remodeled → Hmgcs2 transcription increases, raising Hmgcs2 mRNA and protein, which in turn drives hepatic ketone-body production. Because PPARα acts directly on the Hmgcs2 promoter rather than through a repressive intermediate, the net effect on Hmgcs2 expression relative to the matched unperturbed control is positive.

up PPARA (PPARα, NR1C1) is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that acts as a direct transcriptional activator of Pdk4, so increasing its activity in a matched context raises Pdk4 expression. Mechanism, in order: (1) PPARA binds its response element (PPRE) in the Pdk4 promoter/enhancer as a heterodimer with RXR; (2) with ligand/coactivator recruitment (PGC-1α, etc.), it drives Pdk4 transcription; (3) the resulting PDK4 protein phosphorylates and inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which is the functional readout of PPARA-driven fatty-acid oxidation.
